claims.text: As-deposited non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type thin films or nanoribbons have disordered nanograin structures.
These as-deposited materials contain inherent residual stresses and non-optimized magnetic-domain configurations.
Argon–nitrogen annealing modifies the nanoscale magnetic-domain structure of the films or nanoribbons.
Argon–nitrogen annealing relaxes residual stress and promotes nanoscale atomic reordering.
Stress relaxation and nanoscale reordering reduce magnetic-domain-wall pinning.
Reduced domain-wall pinning produces more uniform domain-wall motion.
Cyclic longitudinal tensile straining fosters a more aligned and homogeneous magnetic-domain structure.
A more aligned, homogeneous domain structure enhances the reversible magnetocaloric response under low-field cycling.
Reduced domain-wall pinning and greater domain homogeneity narrow the magnetic hysteresis loop under low-field cycling.
Untreated as-deposited films or nanoribbons exhibit relatively high magnetic hysteresis.
Untreated as-deposited films or nanoribbons have a diminished magnetocaloric response because of disordered magnetic domains and residual stress.
Relative to the untreated baseline, treated samples will have lower coercivity and smaller hysteresis-loop area.
Relative to the untreated baseline, treated samples will exhibit a larger adiabatic temperature change during low-applied-field cycles.
The predicted treatment effect applies to nanoscale thin films and lithographically patterned nanoribbons under low-field conditions.
The predicted effect may not extend to bulk samples or to conditions in which heat transfer is not rate-limiting.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis describes annealing combined with cyclic tensile straining, whereas the intervention, mechanism, and experiment make straining optional. Thus the tested intervention is not consistently defined, and the design cannot cleanly distinguish annealing alone from the combined treatment.
